scenes.title: Airflow Scheduling, Backfills & Catchup
scenes.narration: This lesson clears up how Airflow schedules DAGs, including the crucial idea of data intervals and how catchup and backfills replay history.

scenes.title: Airflow schedules data intervals
bullets: A run covers a time window, not a single instant
The run fires at the end of its interval
logical_date names the interval being processed
scenes.narration: The most misunderstood part of Airflow is that a run represents a data interval, a window of time, rather than a single instant. Because of this, a run does not fire at the start of its window; it fires at the end, once the data for that window should exist. The logical_date, sometimes still called execution date, labels the interval being processed rather than the wall-clock moment the task runs.

scenes.title: Interval example
steps: Daily DAG, interval Jan 1 00:00 to Jan 2 00:00
scenes.narration: Consider a daily DAG. The interval running from midnight on January first to midnight on January second only completes at the end, so the run actually triggers just after midnight on January second. That run then processes January first's data. Internalizing this end-of-interval timing is what stops the classic off-by-one confusion about which day a run is handling.

scenes.title: Catchup versus manual backfill

left.heading: catchup=True
points: Auto-runs every missed interval since start_date
Can flood the system if start_date is old

right.heading: Backfill (CLI)
points: You choose an explicit date range
Run on demand from the command line

scenes.narration: There are two ways to process past intervals. When catchup is set to true, the scheduler automatically creates a run for every interval between the start date and now, which is powerful but can flood your system if the start date is far in the past. A backfill, by contrast, is something you trigger manually from the command line for an explicit date range, giving you controlled, deliberate reprocessing of history.

scenes.title: Controlling catchup
scenes.code:
with DAG(
    dag_id='sales_daily',
    schedule='0 6 * * *',
    start_date=datetime(2024, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
    max_active_runs=1,
) as dag:
    ...

# Reprocess a range on demand:
# airflow dags backfill sales_daily -s 2024-03-01 -e 2024-03-07
scenes.narration: This DAG uses a cron schedule of six in the morning daily and sets catchup to false, so turning it on does not stampede through every historical interval. Setting max_active_runs to one prevents multiple runs from overlapping. When you genuinely need to reprocess a window, the commented command shows a manual backfill for a specific week, which is the controlled way to replay history on demand.

scenes.text: Default catchup=False and rely on deliberate backfills; write tasks to be idempotent so any interval can be safely rerun.
scenes.narration: The safe default is to leave catchup off and instead trigger deliberate backfills when you need them, and above all to make your tasks idempotent so that any interval can be rerun safely without corrupting or duplicating data.
